01: Imagine putting this character image into a game.
A nice standing image is hard to use if its bag changes sides or its face changes whenever it moves.
We will preserve the character, match its pixel scale and background, then prepare animation and effects.
02: Dividing the work into three stages makes tool selection easier.
Image models propose artwork, while processing tools organize size, colors, and transparency.
Finally, check the assets at their actual size in an engine.
The eight public tools also serve different parts of this process.
You do not need to install every tool at once.
03: Start by fixing the character design.
List the hairstyle, clothing colors, accessories, and bag position that must stay unchanged.
Our reference uses a yellow hair clip, a teal jacket, and a brown bag.
Even with a tool like NovelAI, choose one design before endlessly collecting attractive variations.
04: Next, make a turnaround sheet showing the front, side, and back of the same character.
Give a reference image to ChatGPT image generation and request new views while retaining clothing and proportions.
Generating a sheet does not finish the inspection.
Compare the hair clip, the strap across the back, and the shoes and sleeves side by side.
05: If you need many poses of the same design, use this sheet as the standard for your training data.
Collecting only front views leaves too little information about the side and back.
Combine varied NovelAI poses with ChatGPT turnaround views, correcting or excluding wrong accessories and clothing first.
Twenty to fifty curated images can be a starting experiment, but varied poses and accurate design matter more than the count.
06: LoRA is not the name of a small image folder.
Instead of retraining the whole base model, this adapter learns a weight update using small matrices.
It adds learned character or style information to the base model's existing drawing ability.
Images and captions are training materials; the trained LoRA file is the result.
07: Pixel style and character identity serve different roles.
You can separate how to draw into a style LoRA and whom to draw into a character LoRA.
When training with kohya_ss or OneTrainer, choose a setup compatible with the base model you will generate with.
Files from unrelated model families are not interchangeable merely because they are called LoRAs.
08: Now connect the generation flow in ComfyUI.
A checkpoint contains the base image model.
Load an Illustrious XL model and connect a compatible pixel-style LoRA.
If a character LoRA is ready, chain its node after that.
Pass both MODEL and CLIP connections so the image model and text encoder receive the appropriate changes.
09: Keep the prompt, resolution, and seed fixed when comparing LoRA strengths.
The seed sets the starting point for randomness.
A weak style can resemble an illustration, while excessive strength can damage small accessories or faces.
Change one strength at a time and inspect the features you need to preserve.
Even a fixed seed does not lock poses and accessories, so inspect those changes too.
10: The graph continues beyond the base model and LoRA.
Text is encoded, the sampler progressively denoises a latent image, and the VAE decoder turns it into visible pixels.
Separating these stages makes it easier to retain an image while comparing reduction methods and palettes.
Add a character LoRA once its trained file is available.
11: An image that looks pixelated is not automatically usable game pixel art.
Zooming in may reveal uneven blocks or blurry colors along edges.
Pixel art needs to read one cell at a time on a small logical grid.
Choose the native pixel dimensions used in the game, then normalize the generated image to that grid.
12: PixelArt SakuLike ILXL is described as generating pixels enlarged roughly eightfold.
For that setup, compare reducing 768 by 1344 to 96 by 168.
The goal is not to memorize the numbers.
It is to match the generated pixel structure to the game's grid.
Do not force the same reduction factor onto other models and images.
13: After fixing the grid, inspect the palette.
A palette is the set of colors used by the asset.
Too many near-identical browns add noise, and separately quantizing each frame can make clothing flicker.
Use one palette across the character and check that eyes and accessories remain legible.
The purpose is clearer shapes, not simply the fewest possible colors.
14: A checkerboard painted into the picture is different from an empty background represented by alpha values.
Alternating light and dark backgrounds reveals white fringes and leftover background colors.
Clean contours and stray pixels in an editor like Aseprite, then inspect both the zoomed image and its game display size.
15: Once the character is prepared, match the background.
Generating them independently can produce mismatched colors and furniture proportions.
One approach is outpainting: expand the surroundings of a scene that already contains the character.
Continue the existing colors and object scale, then remove the character from the background layer to make room for a separate sprite.
16: Inspect the pixel scale of the expanded background again.
A one-pixel character outline clashes with furniture edges that appear three pixels thick.
Choose the reduction from the actual grid and match the character's height to the chair.
Repair broken boundaries such as walls, floors, and chair legs.
This stage fixes specific mismatches instead of regenerating the whole background.
17: So far, we have prepared still assets.
These already have many uses in dialogue games and visual novels.
Walking and attacking require additional checks.
Faces must stay consistent, feet must remain grounded, scale must stay stable, and action endpoints must connect.
Now let us see how eight tools divide this remaining work.
18: 2dimg2motion redraws key poses from a reference character and fills in the frames between them.
It establishes preparation, the main action, and recovery first.
Its default pattern includes fourteen frames, but the number alone does not guarantee natural motion.
Check weapons, hands, baseline, and body scale before packaging transparent images and a sheet.
19: sprite-gen supports both image and video routes.
You can assemble pose images into a sheet or extract frames from a short image-generated video.
It connects background removal, frame extraction, loop selection, and atlas construction.
An atlas combines several images on one texture and records their locations.
Distinguishing generation from processing makes the workflow easier to understand.
20: pixelfx fits effects such as fire, explosions, and sword trails.
Code draws pixels over time instead of asking an image model to redraw every frame.
This flame can retain its motion while changing only its palette.
Run the effect directly or export a transparent sprite sheet for sequential playback in the engine.
21: PixelOE belongs to the pixel cleanup stage.
It reinforces important outlines before reducing image size and adjusting colors.
Pixel Snapper is another option for correcting irregular pixel grids and palettes.
Neither should be mistaken for a tool that generates a new walking motion.
Compare actual enlarged results and choose the one that preserves thin lines and faces better.
22: Agent Sprite Forge organizes multiple actions from one master image.
It creates per-action clips such as idle, walk, run, and attack, then handles keying, alignment, loops, and timing.
It also provides map and tile workflows.
Inspect transitions too: height and foot position must not suddenly change when switching from idle to running.
23: Codixel uses references, code, and skeletal control to construct motion.
For example, a long tail or torso can be divided into parts that follow connected control points.
Controlling the same image parts makes targeted motion changes easier.
But a turn cannot automatically reveal an unseen back surface that is absent from the artwork.
That requires additional images or another generation process.
24: Pixelbolt describes colors, shapes, and frames in a JSON text recipe.
An image model did not redraw these spirits.
They were rendered from the same recipe with only the palette changed.
You can make similarly narrow edits to an eye position or a particular frame.
This suits small icons, sprites, and repeated effects that need precise revisions and reproducible output.
25: Sprite Sheet Diffusion is generative research conditioned on a reference character and ordered poses.
It generates character frames for a specified sequence of skeletal poses.
Local inference needs compatible weights and an environment as well as code.
It is therefore different from an editor installed with one click.
Inspect the generated frames for consistent clothing, faces, and motion transitions.
26: Choose tools by first deciding which asset you need.
For still characters and backgrounds, focus on design and pixel cleanup.
For multiple actions, choose among key-pose generation, video frame extraction, and skeletal animation.
Code-based methods work well for effects and small icons with precise edit requirements.
One generative model does not need to perform every stage.
27: Import the finished PNG into the engine for a final check.
In Unity, import it as a sprite and use Point filtering to retain sharp pixel boundaries.
If a sheet contains multiple frames, slice their regions in the correct order.
Pixels Per Unit defines scale in world units, while the pivot is the reference for placement and rotation.
Keep these conventions consistent across a character's actions.
28: Validation goes beyond checking whether a file opens.
Inspect contours on light and dark backgrounds, and compare character scale with scenery.
Play animation at normal speed, then step through frames to find sliding feet, scale changes, and loop seams.
Check whether the action length fits the game too.
An attractive generated clip is not automatically a responsive game action.
29: Finally, separate free public code from generation service costs.
An MIT or Apache tool license does not make connected image and video services free.
Check the base model, LoRA, training images, and output conditions separately.
A code license does not clear rights in another person's character used for training.
Keep model versions, sources, and required notices with your project.
30: Preserve recognizable character design, normalize pixels, colors, transparency, and scale, and validate movement and readability in the game context.
AI can quickly propose candidates and assist repetitive work.
Turning those candidates into assets for our game depends on the process that follows generation.
